The attack failed. I did not take the verifier's word for the Elwes wording: I downloaded the whole Gutenberg Elwes text (pg3800.txt, 531,667 bytes) to the scratchpad and read the proposition in place. Line 8091 reads 'PROP. LXVII.  A free man thinks of death least of all things;' and line 8092 continues 'and his wisdom is a meditation not of death but of life.' That is the proposed quotation with nothing added, nothing dropped, and, crucially, NO COMMA before 'but' — which is exactly where I expected this to break, because the comma'd form 'a meditation not of death, but of life' is the shape the line most often takes when it is quoted second-hand. The proposal carries the uncomma'd Elwes form. Wording confirmed.

LOCATOR CONFIRMED BY BRACKETING, NOT BY TRUST. 'Part IV, Proposition 67' is only right if LXVII sits inside Part IV, and a proposition number alone would not prove that, since the Ethics restarts its numbering in every part. I grepped the part headings: 'PART IV:' is at line 6111 and 'PART V:' at line 8559, and the proposition is at 8091, so it is inside Part IV. LXVII is 67. Both halves of the locator hold. The Proof that follows ('A free man is one who lives under the guidance of reason... his wisdom is a meditation of life. Q.E.D.') is present directly beneath it, which is the structural signature the verifier described and a further check that this is the proposition itself and not a scholiast's gloss or a later summary sentence.

TRANSLATOR CONFIRMED AT THE SOURCE. The file's own header gives 'Author: Benedictus de Spinoza' and 'Translator: R. H. M. Elwes'. The 1883 date is the Bohn/Elwes publication of The Chief Works and is standard. One point worth stating rather than hiding: Elwes's own title page names the author 'Benedict de Spinoza', whereas the source line bylines him 'Baruch Spinoza'. That is not a defect. Rule 5 asks the source to lead with the author's name for use as a byline, and Baruch Spinoza is the name under which he is catalogued and known; the edition parenthesis carries the translator, which is what the translation rule actually requires.

WHAT ELSE I TRIED. (1) Misattribution: not on the brief's trap list, and not a roving line — it is a numbered proposition in a named part of a named work, about as hard-anchored as a citation gets. (2) Speaker: none; Spinoza in his own geometrical voice, no character to name. (3) Scope: Ethics published posthumously 1677, Elwes 1883, both well before 1999; not scripture (it is philosophy about God, which is not the same thing and the Library does not own it), not film, lyric, proverb, business or oratory. (4) Cap and repetition: shipped.js returns shipped [], near [], baruch spinoza at 1 of 3 for the year with his one appearance in month 4, cap 3, not banned. One in a different month does not bar him, and the no-person-twice rule is per month. He is not on personsAtCap.

MECHANICS. Source line 'Baruch Spinoza, Ethics, Part IV, Proposition 67 (trans. R. H. M. Elwes, 1883)' is 77 characters, leads with the name, orders work then locator then translation in parentheses as rule 5 asks, and contains no dash. Quotation ends in a full stop, holds no quote marks of any kind, and is prose kept as prose. Tag Philosophy is the form of the work.

PUBLISHABILITY AND THE SIX A.M. TEST, WHICH IS WHERE I PUSHED HARDEST. This is a line with 'death' in its first clause, dropped on a reader at six in the morning in a month already themed on impermanence, and rule 3 says famous and bleak is out. I still clear it, because the sentence's whole grammatical motion is away from death: the first clause says the free man does not dwell there, the second says the wisdom is of life, and 'life' is the last word a reader's eye lands on. It is the standing answer to the memento mori tradition rather than an instance of it, which makes it the right philosopher's line for a month of elegies. No wound, no dying described, nothing needing a warning.

ONE THING THE EDITOR SHOULD WEIGH. The note is empty, and this line benefits from one more than the others do, because a reader who meets it cold may hear it as a refusal to think about death at all. Spinoza's point is narrower: the free man's meditation is on living, not that death is not to be faced. A one-sentence note to that effect would keep the line from being read as evasion. Not a refutation; the citation is sound.
